turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. [Name]. Yeah, thanks for seeing me. Well, what brings me in... it's mostly work stuff. I'm a supervisor for a sales team, and I just—I keep making these really dumb mistakes on our sales reports. 

It's so frustrating because, I mean, I'm the supervisor, right? I'm supposed to be the one catching this stuff for my guys. But I'll be looking right at our team dashboard, staring directly at the screen with all the weekly metrics, and I'll just copy the completely wrong numbers over to the final report. Or we have these procedures, like these specific compliance checklists for client accounts that I have to review and sign off on, and I'll just completely miss a line I was supposed to check. 

And the craziest part is, I could swear I went over it. Like, I'll sit there, look at the form, tell myself I checked everything, and then my boss will email me later and point out that I skipped a whole section. It's driving me crazy because I'm not an idiot, you know? I worked hard to get this promotion, I know how to read a spreadsheet, but these little details just keep slipping past me. I even tried printing the reports out recently, thinking that holding the actual paper would help me catch the errors better than looking at a monitor, but then I just make the exact same mistakes on the physical copy. Which almost feels worse somehow, because then I have this piece of paper on my desk proving I looked right at it and still messed it up...

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly describes making careless mistakes on sales reports, copying wrong numbers, and missing details on checklists despite reviewing them.

turns.doctor_question: Besides these mistakes with details at work, have you noticed any other changes in your thinking—like trouble remembering things, difficulty finding words, or feeling confused about things that used to be clear to you?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my memory is fine, I think. Well, I guess I should say I don't feel confused or anything like that. It's not like I'm sitting there staring at the screen and don't know what a spreadsheet is, or can't remember how to do my job, or can't find the words to explain things to my team. Like I said, I'm a supervisor, I'm talking to my guys all day, explaining metrics, giving feedback, going over their numbers. I'm sharp when it comes to that stuff. 

It's really just the... the execution part, I guess you could call it. The actual sitting down and making sure the little boxes are checked and the numbers match up perfectly. It's not a memory thing, and it's definitely not confusion. I know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing, and I understand the process completely. I've been doing this kind of work for a long time, right out of high school basically, working my way up. So I know the ropes inside and out. It's just that when it comes down to the actual moment of looking at the detail and recording it, my brain just... skips a beat, or glosses over it. But no, to answer your question, no trouble with words, no memory loss, no confusion. I'm completely clear-headed about what I'm doing, which is honestly why it's so incredibly frustrating when I mess up. If I was confused, it would almost make more sense, you know? But I'm not.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reiterates that their brain 'glosses over' details when recording them, confirming inattention to details.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly denies having memory issues or forgetfulness.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly denies having trouble finding words to explain things to their team.
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient explicitly denies feeling confused, having memory loss, or lacking clear-headedness.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any changes in your balance, coordination, or the way you move? Or any tremors, stiffness, or difficulty with physical tasks?
turns.patient_response:
No, nothing like that at all. I mean, my balance is totally fine. I still play in a rec softball league on the weekends—well, when I actually remember to check the schedule and show up on time, but that's a whole other thing. Physically, though, I'm good. I run the bases fine, I don't feel stiff or anything. I'm 36, so I mean, sure, I get a little sore if I slide into second base too hard, but that's just getting older, right? 

But no tremors, my hands don't shake when I'm holding a pen or trying to read those printed reports I told you about. I can type just fine, my coordination is completely normal. I'm walking around the sales floor all day, checking in on my team, pacing around while I'm on calls with clients. I've never tripped over my own feet or felt like my body wasn't doing what I wanted it to do. It's really just my brain that feels like it's misfiring when I have to sit still and look at a spreadsheet. Physically, I feel completely normal. I haven't noticed any changes in how I move or anything like that. It's all just... up here, you know? Just the mental slip-ups with the details. But physically, my body works exactly the way it always has.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly mentions having 'mental slip-ups with the details.'
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes their brain 'misfiring' when having to sit still and look at a spreadsheet, indicating difficulty sustaining attention on tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient notes they struggle to remember to check their softball schedule and show up on time, indicating forgetfulness in daily activities.

turns.doctor_question: When did you first start noticing these kinds of mistakes with details—was it something that's been happening your whole life, or is this something more recent that started around the time you got promoted to supervisor?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask it exactly like that, because I've been thinking about this a lot lately. Like, really racking my brain trying to figure out when exactly this all started going off the rails. And honestly... it's been a real problem since I moved into the supervisor role. That was about... let's see, it's been about a year and two months now. 

Before that, when I was just on the floor doing the actual selling? I mean, sure, maybe I wasn't the most organized guy in the world, maybe my desk was a little messy, but it didn't matter in the same way. When you're just selling, you're on the phone, you're pitching, you're moving fast, you know? The energy is high, and you're just onto the next call, the next lead. If I didn't log a call perfectly in the CRM, it wasn't the end of the world. 

But then I got this promotion—which, like I said, I worked really hard for. I was top of the leaderboard for like six months straight to get it. And I was so excited. But the job is just... different. Suddenly I'm not the one making the calls, I'm the one reviewing the calls. I'm the one looking at the spreadsheets, doing the QA on the compliance checklists, making sure the team's metrics are all tallied up perfectly for the regional manager. And it's like, almost immediately after I took the job, maybe a month or two in, once the initial excitement wore off and I really had to settle into the routine of it, that's when these mistakes just started piling up. 

So yeah, a year and two months of this. And it's just been this slow build of frustration ever since. Because I keep telling myself I'll do better next week, I'll double-check everything, I'll drink an extra cup of coffee before I do the reports... and then, boom, my boss is emailing me again about a copied-and-pasted error. So it really is tied to this new role. It's like this job requires a specific kind of focus that I just... I don't know, I just can't seem to hold onto for more than five minutes at a time.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes making careless mistakes that pile up, specifically mentioning copied-and-pasted errors in reports.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly states an inability to hold focus for more than five minutes at a time on tasks requiring specific focus.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient admits to historically not being the most organized person and having a messy desk.

turns.doctor_question: When you're not at work—like when you're at home in the evening, or playing softball on the weekend, or doing things you enjoy—do you notice the same kind of trouble focusing on details, or does that problem seem to only happen when you're dealing with work tasks?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, not really. I mean, I haven't noticed anything like that when I'm off the clock. It really just seems to be a work thing, specifically with those reports and the administrative side of the job. 

Like, you mentioned the softball league—I actually manage the lineup for our team. You'd think that would be a lot of details, right? Making sure everyone gets equal playing time, figuring out the batting order, keeping track of who is playing what position in which inning so nobody gets stuck in the outfield the whole game. But I have zero problems with that. None at all. I can rattle off everyone's stats, I know exactly who hits well against certain pitchers, and I never mess up the scorecard. It's because it's happening right in front of me, it's fast, and I'm into it, you know? 

And at home, it's the same thing. I don't have those weird mental blank-outs. If I'm working on something around the house—like lately I've been doing some landscaping in the backyard, building these raised planter boxes—I measure everything out, I get all the angles right, I don't make careless mistakes. Sure, I might misplace my tape measure for five minutes or forget to grab a box of screws while I'm at Home Depot, but everybody does that. I'm not, like, cutting the wood two inches too short because I glossed over the numbers on the tape measure. 

So it really just seems isolated to the job. Which, honestly, makes me feel incredibly guilty. Because I sit there at my desk and think, "Why can I perfectly organize a nine-inning softball game with fifteen different guys subbing in and out, but I can't copy a sales metric from one column to another without screwing it up?" It makes it feel like I just don't care about my job, or like I'm not trying, but I *do* care. I care a lot. I worked so hard for that promotion. But yeah, outside of work, doing my own thing, I don't notice any trouble with details at all. It's just when I'm staring at those work checklists.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient confirms making careless mistakes with details at work, such as copying sales metrics, although they deny this happens outside of work.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient admits to misplacing items like their tape measure, even though they minimize it as something 'everybody does'.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient admits to being forgetful in daily activities, such as forgetting to grab screws at the hardware store.
symptom_reasoning.S030: The patient expresses feeling 'incredibly guilty' about their inability to manage details at work despite caring a lot about their job.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient denies difficulty organizing tasks outside of work, noting they can 'perfectly organize a nine-inning softball game'.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient demonstrates clear interest and enjoyment in hobbies like softball and landscaping, indicating no loss of interest in activities.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: In the year or so before you got promoted to supervisor—before these detail mistakes started happening—did you have any significant illnesses, head injuries, accidents, or any major changes in your health? Or have you started any new medications or supplements around that time?
turns.patient_response:
No, honestly, nothing at all. I mean, I'm a pretty healthy guy, you know? I don't really get sick. Maybe I'll catch a minor cold here or there in the winter when everyone else in the office is coughing, but definitely no major illnesses, no surgeries, nothing that would put me in the hospital or keep me out of work. 

And no head injuries, thank God. I mean, I play softball, like I said, and sometimes things get a little intense out there, but I've never taken a line drive to the head or had a concussion or anything crazy like that. I drive safe, haven't been in any car accidents. It's actually kind of frustrating, in a weird, messed-up way, because if I *had* hit my head or something, at least I'd have a tangible excuse for why my brain is suddenly refusing to cooperate with these spreadsheets, you know? Like, I could tell my boss, "Hey, sorry I messed up the compliance checklist, I got a concussion last month." But no, my health has been exactly the same as it's always been. 

And as for medications, I don't take anything. I mean, I'll take some ibuprofen if my knees or my back are acting up after a weekend tournament, and I guess I have this generic multivitamin sitting in my bathroom cabinet that I take whenever I actually remember it's there, but I haven't started any new prescriptions or weird internet supplements or anything like that. I don't even really drink those crazy pre-workout powders or energy drinks, just my regular morning coffee. 

So yeah, physically, medically, everything leading up to the promotion and even right now has been totally, completely boring and normal. Which, you know, just brings me back to square one, sitting there staring at my screen, trying to figure out why I'm suddenly dropping the ball at work when absolutely everything else in my life and my health is perfectly fine. It's just baffling.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient references messing up a compliance checklist, struggling with spreadsheets, and dropping the ball at work, confirming ongoing issues with detail-oriented mistakes.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Going back further—when you were in school, or even earlier in your sales career when you were doing the actual selling on the phones, did you ever have any trouble focusing on detailed tasks, or did teachers or supervisors ever mention that you were careless with details, even if it wasn't causing you major problems at the time?
turns.patient_response:
You know, it’s crazy you bring up school, because... well, if I’m being completely honest, yeah, I was absolutely like this as a kid, too. It’s funny, my mom—she’s one of those people who keeps absolutely everything, right? Like, she’s got these plastic storage tubs in her attic full of every report card, every drawing, every little scrap of paper from when I was growing up. And she actually still talks about it to this day. She’ll bring up these notes she used to get from my teachers back in elementary school, and it’s like... it’s almost exactly what my boss is saying now, just the third-grade version of it. 

The teachers were always writing home saying that I rushed through my work. Like, I’d just blast through a worksheet as fast as humanly possible so I could be done with it, and of course, I’d get all the details wrong or skip half the questions. And the homework—man, I swear I would sit at the kitchen table, I would do the math problems, I’d put it in my folder, and then somehow between the front door and the classroom, it would just vanish. I lost so much homework it drove my parents insane. 

But it wasn’t even just the work itself, it was... well, everything else, too. The notes were always like, "He talks out of turn constantly." I was always just blurting things out, interrupting the teacher, making jokes with the kid sitting next to me. And they were always, always having to remind me to stay in my seat. I just couldn't stay seated. I’d be up sharpening my pencil for the fourth time in an hour, or I’d just be standing next to my desk instead of sitting in the chair, and I wouldn't even realize I was doing it until the teacher called me out and told me to sit back down. 

So, yeah... I guess when I really look back at it, the teachers definitely noticed it. It just sort of... faded into the background for a long time, especially when I got into sales. Because when you're just pitching on the phones, being a fast-talking guy who can't sit still is actually kind of a superpower, you know? You're just dialing and moving and the energy is good. But yeah, back in school? The teachers were definitely dealing with the exact same careless, rushed stuff my boss is dealing with now.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient states he would rush through work and get all the details wrong or skip questions.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions frequently losing his homework between home and the classroom.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes being unable to stay seated in class, frequently standing by his desk or getting up.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient notes that teachers said he talked out of turn constantly and describes himself as a fast-talking guy.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states he was always blurting things out in class.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient admits to frequently interrupting the teacher.
